statement: A meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for human longevity (survival to the 90th/99th percentile) found only two genome-wide-significant loci: APOE/TOMM40 (chr19) and a locus at 5q33.3 (near EBF1); polygenic longevity scores also captured GWAS signal for parental lifespan.
effect_size: Two genome-wide-significant loci (APOE/TOMM40, 5q33.3); APOE is by far the strongest. Most candidate longevity loci did NOT replicate.
population: Meta-analysis of GWAS, ~36k long-lived cases + ~365k controls, European ancestry

provenance.primary: Deelen, Evans, Arking et al. — 'A meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies identifies multiple longevity genes', Nat Commun 2019

confidence_notes: Meta-analysis of OBSERVATIONAL genetic association (not interventional). The headline is deflationary: beyond APOE, almost nothing replicates at genome-wide significance. Extends the centenarian-gwas-polygenic claim in B-claims.json with the actual meta result.

statement: A GWAS of ~1 million parental lifespans implicated loci tied to smoking behavior (CHRNA3/5), lipid metabolism (LPA, APOE, CETP), blood pressure, diabetes, and immune/cancer pathways — i.e., human lifespan genetics is largely the genetics of common age-related disease, not a separate 'longevity program'.
effect_size: ~12 genome-wide-significant lifespan loci; effects translate to months of life expectancy per allele; dominated by smoking + cardiometabolic disease genes.
population: UK Biobank + LifeGen, ~1,012,240 parental lifespans, European ancestry

provenance.primary: Timmers, Mounier et al. — 'Genomics of 1 million parent lifespans...', eLife 2019

confidence_notes: Kin-cohort GWAS (association). Reframes 'longevity genes' as mostly disease/behavior genes — tempers the search for dedicated longevity loci.

statement: A genetic signature of ~281 SNPs distinguished centenarians from controls with ~60-85% accuracy and defined longevity-associated genetic subgroups — but this paper is the corrected re-publication after the original 2010 Science report was retracted for a genotyping-array artifact.
effect_size: 281-SNP model, AUC ~0.6 (whole sample) up to ~0.85 (oldest/901+). Predictive in-sample; weak generalization.
population: New England Centenarian Study: ~800-1000 centenarians vs controls

provenance.primary: Sebastiani, Solovieff, Perls et al. — 'Genetic Signatures of Exceptional Longevity in Humans', PLoS ONE 2012

confidence_notes: CAUTIONARY TALE: the 2010 Science version (Sebastiani 2010) was RETRACTED due to a technical genotyping artifact on a subset of arrays; the 2012 PLoS ONE version re-ran with corrected genotyping and reduced (but non-zero) accuracy. Index this as a reproducibility object, not a settled predictor.

statement: Ashkenazi-Jewish centenarians and their offspring show a distinctive lipoprotein phenotype (large LDL/HDL particle size) linked to a CETP variant (and APOC3) — among the first specific gene-longevity associations beyond APOE.
effect_size: Homozygous CETP I405V (VV) more frequent in probands/offspring; associated with larger lipoprotein particles, lower CVD/dementia.
population: Longevity Genes Project: Ashkenazi centenarians, offspring, controls (Albert Einstein, Barzilai)

provenance.primary: Barzilai, Atzmon, Schechter et al. — 'Unique Lipoprotein Phenotype and Genotype Associated With Exceptional Longevity', JAMA 2003

confidence_notes: Candidate-gene case-control in a founder population — CETP association is population/context-specific and not consistently replicated; pharmacological CETP inhibition has NOT reproduced a longevity benefit (see conflict).

statement: Accelerated DNA-methylation age of blood (DNAm age minus chronological age) predicts higher all-cause mortality independent of chronological age and classical risk factors — the first demonstration that an epigenetic clock tracks death risk.
effect_size: ~5% higher mortality risk per year of epigenetic age acceleration (pooled across 4 cohorts).
population: 4 longitudinal cohorts (Lothian Birth Cohorts + others), ~5000 individuals

provenance.primary: Marioni, Shah, McRae et al. — 'DNA methylation age of blood predicts all-cause mortality in later life', Genome Biol 2015

confidence_notes: Cohort association (prediction), not causal proof methylation drives death. Built on the first-gen Hannum clock; second-gen clocks (GrimAge, see B-claims) predict mortality more strongly.

statement: A meta-analysis pooling DNA-methylation clock data across multiple cohorts confirmed that epigenetic age acceleration robustly predicts time-to-death, establishing the epigenetic clock as a reproducible mortality biomarker.
effect_size: Each ~5-year increase in epigenetic age acceleration associated with materially higher mortality hazard; replicated across cohorts.
population: Meta-analysis, ~13,000 individuals across 13 cohorts

provenance.primary: Chen, Marioni, Colicino et al. — 'DNA methylation-based measures of biological age: meta-analysis predicting time to death', Aging 2016

confidence_notes: META-tier for the predictive (association) claim. Does NOT establish that methylation changes are causal in aging — only that they forecast death better than chance.

statement: A consensus review classifies epigenetic clocks into first-generation (Horvath, Hannum — trained on chronological age) and second-generation (PhenoAge, GrimAge — trained on clinical/mortality outcomes), and concludes clocks are CORRELATIVE biomarkers whose causal role in aging is unestablished.
effect_size: Framework + recommendations; flags that different clocks capture different signals and correlate imperfectly with each other.
population: Multi-author consensus / methodological review

provenance.primary: Bell, Lowe, Adams et al. — 'DNA methylation aging clocks: challenges and recommendations', Genome Biol 2019

confidence_notes: The discipline document for this sub-domain: separates clock GENERATION and warns against reading a methylation correlate as a cause of aging. Mechanism/review tier.

statement: Original epigenetic clocks have poor technical reliability (low test-retest ICC at individual CpGs), inflating apparent intervention effects; principal-component (PC) versions of the clocks dramatically improve reliability and are recommended for longitudinal/clinical-trial use.
effect_size: PC-clocks raise test-retest reliability (ICC) to >0.95 vs as low as ~0.6-0.8 for original clocks; reduces spurious 'age reversal' from measurement noise.
population: Technical re-analysis across multiple methylation datasets (Yale, Levine/Higgins-Chen)

provenance.primary: Higgins-Chen, Thrush, Wang et al. — 'A computational solution for bolstering reliability of epigenetic clocks', Nat Aging 2022

confidence_notes: Crucial methodological caveat: many published 'epigenetic age reversal' effects are within the measurement noise of the original clocks. Validity > effect-size here.

statement: In a 1-year, single-arm pilot (TRIIM, n=9 men) a regimen of recombinant growth hormone + DHEA + metformin was associated with thymus regeneration and a ~1.5-2.5-year decrease in epigenetic (DNAm) age.
effect_size: Mean epigenetic age reversal ~2.5y (some clocks) over 12 months; thymic fat→tissue conversion on MRI.
population: 9 healthy men aged 51-65, open-label single-arm

provenance.primary: Fahy, Brooke, Watson et al. — 'Reversal of epigenetic aging and immunosenescent trends in humans', Aging Cell 2019

confidence_notes: Widely cited as 'first human age reversal' but it is a TINY UNCONTROLLED PILOT; the GH arm confounds; the effect size is near the reliability limit flagged by Higgins-Chen 2022. Do NOT treat as efficacy.

statement: A universal pan-mammalian DNA-methylation clock built across 348 species predicts age in all of them from conserved CpG sites, showing that methylation-based aging is an evolutionarily conserved feature of mammalian biology, not a human statistical artifact.
effect_size: Single clock generalizes across 348 mammal species; conserved age-related CpGs map to development/polycomb targets.
population: ~11,000 samples, 348 mammalian species (Mammalian Methylation Consortium, Horvath/Lu)

provenance.primary: Lu, Fei, Haghani et al. — 'Universal DNA methylation age across mammalian tissues', Nat Aging 2023

confidence_notes: Strengthens the case that the epigenetic clock reflects a conserved biological process (vs pure curve-fitting). Cross-species/animal evidence — still a correlate, not a demonstrated cause of aging.

statement: The human plasma proteome changes NON-LINEARLY across the lifespan in three distinct waves of differential expression peaking at roughly ages 34, 60, and 78; a proteomic clock predicts chronological age and deviations track health.
effect_size: ~1379 proteins change with age; 3 'waves'; proteomic clock predicts age within ~3 years.
population: Cross-sectional plasma from ~4,263 adults aged 18-95

provenance.primary: Lehallier, Gate, Schaum, Wyss-Coray et al. — 'Undulating changes in human plasma proteome profiles across the lifespan', Nat Med 2019

confidence_notes: Cross-sectional (the 'waves' are inferred across people, not followed within individuals). Landmark for the idea that aging is non-linear and proteomically measurable.

statement: Organ-specific plasma-proteomic aging clocks reveal that organs age at different rates within one person; ~1 in 5 healthy adults shows strongly accelerated aging in at least one organ, and accelerated organ age predicts that organ's future disease and mortality.
effect_size: Accelerated heart age → ~2.5x heart-failure risk; accelerated brain/vasculature age → Alzheimer's risk; organ age adds prognostic info beyond chronological age.
population: ~5,676 adults across multiple cohorts (Stanford, Wyss-Coray lab)

provenance.primary: Oh, Rutledge, Nachun, Wyss-Coray et al. — 'Organ aging signatures in the plasma proteome track health and disease', Nature 2023

confidence_notes: Cohort prediction. Reframes 'biological age' as organ-specific rather than a single number. Surrogate/biomarker endpoints, not interventional.

statement: Deep longitudinal multi-omic profiling of individuals over years identifies distinct 'ageotypes' — people age predominantly along different molecular axes (metabolic, immune, hepatic, nephrotic) — so a single biological-age number obscures system-specific aging.
effect_size: ≥4 ageotype classes; individuals show consistent personal aging trajectories across visits.
population: 43 adults followed 2-4 years, dense multi-omics (Snyder lab, Stanford)

provenance.primary: Ahadi, Zhou, Snyder et al. — 'Personal aging markers and ageotypes revealed by deep longitudinal profiling', Nat Med 2020

confidence_notes: Small n but longitudinal (within-person). Supports personalized, multi-axis aging over a single clock value.

statement: A deep-learning 'inflammatory aging clock' (iAge) built from circulating immune markers tracks multimorbidity, frailty, and immunosenescence; the chemokine CXCL9 emerges as a dominant driver of age-related systemic inflammation.
effect_size: iAge associates with multimorbidity, frailty, cardiovascular aging; CXCL9 identified as a central node.
population: 1000 Immunomes Project + validation cohorts (Stanford, Furman lab)

provenance.primary: Sayed, Huang, Furman et al. — 'An inflammatory aging clock (iAge)...', Nat Aging 2021

confidence_notes: Operationalizes inflammaging (see B-claims) as a measurable proteomic clock. Association/prediction, points to CXCL9 as a mechanistic candidate.

statement: The gut microbiota remodels with extreme age: centenarians show reduced diversity, loss of short-chain-fatty-acid (SCFA)-producing/anti-inflammatory taxa (e.g., Faecalibacterium prausnitzii), and enrichment of pathobionts, paralleling rising inflammatory markers ('inflammaging').
effect_size: Distinct centenarian community structure; loss of butyrate producers; correlated rise in IL-6/IL-8.
population: Young adults, elderly (~70y), centenarians — Italian cohort (Biagi/Franceschi)

provenance.primary: Biagi, Nylund, Franceschi et al. — 'Through Ageing, and Beyond: Gut Microbiota and Inflammatory Status in Seniors and Centenarians', PLoS ONE 2010

confidence_notes: Cross-sectional correlation (composition ↔ inflammation); cannot tell whether dysbiosis causes inflammaging or reflects diet/drugs/reduced motility in the very old.

statement: Low gut microbial gene richness ('low gene count' enterotype) is associated with greater adiposity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and a more inflammatory phenotype than high-richness microbiomes.
effect_size: ~23% of individuals 'low gene count'; worse metabolic markers; partly modifiable by diet.
population: 292 Danish adults, metagenomic sequencing (MetaHIT)

provenance.primary: Le Chatelier, Nielsen, Ehrlich et al. — 'Richness of human gut microbiome correlates with metabolic markers', Nature 2013

confidence_notes: Cross-sectional association linking microbiome richness to metabolic health (a longevity-relevant intermediate). Not causal; diet is a major confounder/lever.

statement: In healthy aging the gut microbiome becomes increasingly UNIQUE to the individual (drifting away from a shared Bacteroides-dominated core); higher uniqueness is associated with favorable metabolites and predicts survival, whereas less-healthy older adults retain the 'average' microbiome.
effect_size: Microbiome 'uniqueness' rises from mid-life; high uniqueness associated with ~lower mortality over 4-year follow-up in the healthy.
population: ~9,000 adults across 3 cohorts (Arivale + validation, Gibbons/Wilmanski, ISB)

provenance.primary: Wilmanski, Diener, Gibbons et al. — 'Gut microbiome pattern reflects healthy ageing and predicts survival in humans', Nat Metab 2021

confidence_notes: Cohort prediction. The 'uniqueness' signal is health-state-dependent (absent in unhealthy aging), which is itself evidence that microbiome is partly a readout of host health.

statement: Centenarian gut microbiomes are enriched for bacteria that produce unusual bile acids (notably isoallo-lithocholic acid, isoalloLCA) with potent activity against Gram-positive pathogens including C. difficile — a candidate mechanism for resistance to enteric infection in the very old.
effect_size: isoalloLCA among the most potent endogenous antimicrobials identified; producing taxa enriched in centenarians vs younger/elderly controls.
population: Japanese centenarians vs controls + isolate/gnotobiotic mechanistic work (Honda lab)

provenance.primary: Sato, Atarashi, Plichta, Honda et al. — 'Novel bile acid biosynthetic pathways are enriched in the microbiome of centenarians', Nature 2021
provenance.surfaced_via: OpenAlex direct-DOI Sato centenarian bile acids

confidence_notes: Mechanism with isolate/gnotobiotic backing (stronger than pure correlation). Whether isoalloLCA contributes to longevity itself (vs infection resistance) is not shown.

statement: A deep-learning 'microbiome aging clock' predicts an individual's chronological age from gut taxonomic profiles, demonstrating that community composition carries an age signal usable as a biomarker.
effect_size: Predicts age with mean absolute error ~6 years from ~95 microbial features.
population: ~4,000 gut metagenome/16S samples, healthy individuals (Galkin/Zhavoronkov, Insilico/Deep Longevity)

provenance.primary: Galkin, Mamoshina, Zhavoronkov et al. — 'Human Gut Microbiome Aging Clock Based on Taxonomic Profiling and Deep Learning', iScience 2020

confidence_notes: Biomarker/predictor only (and from a commercial longevity-testing group). A composition-age correlation is not evidence the microbiome drives aging.

statement: Short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate, acetate) produced by bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber are the primary colonocyte fuel and support gut-barrier integrity and regulatory-T-cell/anti-inflammatory tone; age-related loss of SCFA producers is a proposed mechanistic link from dysbiosis to inflammaging.
effect_size: Butyrate fuels colonocytes, induces colonic Tregs (FOXP3), strengthens tight junctions; SCFA decline tracks reduced fiber-fermenters in aging.
population: Mouse mechanistic + human associative

provenance.primary: Furman et al. — 'Chronic inflammation in the etiology of disease across the life span', Nat Med 2019 (synthesis); SCFA/Treg: Smith/Arpaia 2013

confidence_notes: MECHANISM (gut barrier + immune tone). The 'fiber→SCFA→longevity' chain is biologically grounded but the human OUTCOME (lifespan) is inferential.

statement: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is maternally inherited, present in high and variable copy number, and frequently heteroplasmic (a mix of mutant and wild-type genomes); a pathogenic mutation only causes dysfunction once its heteroplasmy fraction crosses a tissue-specific threshold.
effect_size: Threshold effect (often ~60-90% mutant load) before biochemical defect manifests; mtDNA mutation rate >> nuclear DNA.
population: Human mitochondrial genetics synthesis (Wallace)

provenance.primary: Wallace & Chalkia — 'Mitochondrial DNA Genetics and the Heteroplasmy Conundrum in Evolution and Disease', Cold Spring Harb Perspect Biol 2013

confidence_notes: Foundational mitochondrial-genetics mechanism and a direct UP-link to the biophysics canon. Threshold/heteroplasmy is the key concept under mtDNA-aging claims.

statement: Mice engineered with a proofreading-deficient mitochondrial DNA polymerase (POLG 'mutator' mice) accumulate mtDNA point mutations and deletions and develop a premature-aging phenotype with reduced lifespan — causal evidence that mtDNA mutation load can drive aging features.
effect_size: 3-5x increased mtDNA mutation burden; premature greying, alopecia, kyphosis, osteoporosis, anemia, reduced lifespan.
population: PolgA(D257A) mutator mice

provenance.primary: Trifunovic, Wredenberg, Larsson et al. — 'Premature ageing in mice expressing defective mitochondrial DNA polymerase', Nature 2004

confidence_notes: Animal outcome. Powerful proof-of-principle but the mutation loads FAR exceed those seen in normal human aging — limits direct translation (see conflict).

statement: An independent mtDNA mutator-mouse line confirmed the premature-aging phenotype and showed it is driven by mtDNA-mutation-induced APOPTOSIS and tissue loss rather than by elevated reactive-oxygen-species damage — challenging the ROS-centric free-radical theory of aging.
effect_size: Increased apoptotic markers in high-turnover tissues; little evidence of increased oxidative damage.
population: POLG mutator mice (Prolla/Kujoth lab)

provenance.primary: Kujoth, Hiona, Prolla et al. — 'Mitochondrial DNA Mutations, Oxidative Stress, and Apoptosis in Mammalian Aging', Science 2005

confidence_notes: Decouples mtDNA-mutation aging from the naive free-radical/ROS theory (cross-links to the free-radical conflict in B-CONFLICTS). Mechanism via apoptosis, animal model.

statement: Somatic mtDNA mutations and heteroplasmy accumulate clonally with age in human post-mitotic and high-turnover tissues (brain, muscle, colonic crypts, substantia nigra), producing mosaic respiratory-chain-deficient cells — but their causal contribution to NORMAL human aging (vs being a correlate) remains debated.
effect_size: Age-dependent rise in mtDNA deletions/point mutations and COX-deficient cells; loads in normal aging usually below the mutator-mouse range.
population: Human tissue studies + reviews (Bratić & Larsson synthesis)

provenance.primary: Bratić & Larsson — 'The role of mitochondria in aging', J Clin Invest 2013 (review); supported by human single-cell/tissue mtDNA studies

confidence_notes: Observational accumulation is well-established; the leap to 'mtDNA mutations cause normal aging' is the contested step (loads, threshold, clonal expansion). Cross-links to free-radical-theory conflict.

statement: A field consensus holds that no omics biomarker of aging (epigenetic, proteomic, metabolomic, microbiomic) is yet validated as a surrogate endpoint that reliably MOVES with interventions and predicts their clinical benefit; standardized validation frameworks are an explicit open need.
effect_size: Consensus/roadmap; defines criteria a biomarker must meet (reliability, responsiveness, predictiveness) — most current aging biomarkers fail ≥1.
population: Biomarkers of Aging Consortium / multi-author consensus

provenance.primary: Moqri, Herzog, Gladyshev et al. — 'Biomarkers of aging for the identification and evaluation of longevity interventions', Cell 2023

confidence_notes: The honest meta-statement for all of Domain C's biomarkers: predictive ≠ validated surrogate. Anchors the 'which clock is valid' conflict at the consensus level.
